intro: On 1 September 1686 three Siamese ambassadors walked the length of the Grande Galerie at Versailles toward a silver throne, carrying a letter from King Narai of Ayutthaya, bowing so low and so often that the court talked of nothing else, and then backed all the way out so as never to turn from Louis XIV. The man at their head, Kosa Pan (Ok-phra Wisut Sunthon), was a foster brother of the king who sent him. For six months France looked at him, and he, with his scribes, looked at France. The embassy was one half of a two-way traffic. In 1685 Louis XIV had sent the Chevalier de Chaumont to Siam, partly to win trade and partly in the hope, encouraged by missionaries and by Narai's Greek favourite Constantine Phaulkon, that the king might become Catholic. The French aims were plain: converts, commercial privileges, and, as it turned out, garrisons at Bangkok and Mergui. Kosa Pan sailed home with those garrisons in 1687, and in 1688 a palace revolution led by Phetracha killed Phaulkon, saw Narai die and drove the French out. The record is lopsided, and this chapter says so. Kosa Pan's own report to his king is lost except for a fortnight at Brest, found by accident in a Paris mission archive in the 1980s; his letters of thanks from the Cape survive in French colonial files. Almost everything else about the Siamese in France was written by their hosts: the courtier Dangeau's terse diary, the Mercure galant's flattering serial, a master of ceremonies' later memoir. On the Siamese side the royal archives perished in 1767, and the chronicles that survive were compiled later. The reciprocal gaze is richer. Choisy's daily letters and Chaumont's and Tachard's relations describe Narai's court in 1685; La Loubère, in 1687, studied Siam like an ethnographer and recorded what Siamese who had been to France said about French women, pictures and prices. Ok-khun Chamnan, a Siamese envoy wrecked on the South African coast in 1686, reached Europe in 1688; his story survives only as a Jesuit retold it. A French officer's prison diary from Mergui, printed in London, closes the story from inside the revolution. Laid side by side, these eyes show two courts performing for each other: France measuring the envoys by their admiration, the envoys measuring France in feet and counting its trees, and each side's records about the other shaped by what it wanted. Where a date or detail rests on secondary summary rather than the text, it is marked approximate.

title: The Paradise of the Infidels: An Ottoman Envoy in Regency France
eyes: Louis de Rouvroy, duc de Saint-Simon
places: Aboard French ships, in quarantine at Toulon and Maguelone, on the Canal du Midi, then six months in Paris and its royal
Istanbul, reporting to the Hofkriegsrat in Vienna
Montpellier and the Languedoc towns on the route
Montpellier, overseeing the second quarantine and the passage through Languedoc
Paris, Palais-Royal and the foreign ministry
Paris, Porte Saint-Antoine to the Hôtel des Ambassadeurs
Pera, Istanbul, writing to Secretaries of State Craggs and Carteret
intro: In October 1720 an Ottoman treasurer of about fifty, Yirmisekiz Çelebi Mehmed Efendi, sailed from Istanbul on a French ship with a letter from Sultan Ahmed III for the ten-year-old Louis XV. The Peace of Passarowitz had ended a long war with the Habsburgs, and the Grand Vizier Nevşehirli Damat İbrahim Pasha, encouraged by the French ambassador Bonnac, wanted a closer look at the power that had long been the Porte's partner in the West. He arrived at the worst possible moment. Plague had broken out in Marseille, Law's financial system had just collapsed, and the foreign minister Dubois was writing that a cancelled embassy would suit him. Mehmed was held in quarantine at Toulon, shipped to Sète, and shut for forty days on the island of Maguelone, before being carried along the Canal du Midi to Toulouse and Bordeaux and up to Paris. He entered the capital on 16 March 1721, was received by the eleven-year-old king at the Tuileries on 21 March, and stayed until early August, visiting Versailles, Marly, the Observatory, the Gobelins, the opera and the royal library. His sefaretname, written after his return for the Grand Vizier, is the traveller's side of this chapter: a careful, often admiring account of canals, mirrors, machines and gardens. Many historians have linked it to the French-style pleasure gardens of the Tulip Era and, through his son Said Efendi, to the printing press İbrahim Müteferrika opened in Istanbul in 1727; others point out that the text never mentions printing and argue that the embassy's diplomatic results were slight. Both positions are given here. The hosts' record is mostly not diaries. It is administrative letters from the commander and intendant of Languedoc, who counted candles and cotton bales; dispatches from the British and Habsburg ambassadors in Paris and Istanbul, who watched the Turk as a possible ally of France; the Paris press, which saw costume and spectacle; and the memoir Saint-Simon wrote decades later. These are dated records of the visitor rather than personal journals, and are marked as such. Laid side by side, they show one traveller seen at once as a guest, a health risk, a bill, a spectacle and a spy, while he himself was looking at France as a model, a puzzle and a warning about how his own words would be read at home.

intro: In July 1774 the Adventure, Tobias Furneaux's consort ship on Cook's second voyage, came into Spithead carrying a young man from Raiatea named Mai, written by the English as Omai or Omiah. He had joined the ship at Huahine the year before. Within days he had been handed by Lord Sandwich, First Lord of the Admiralty, to Joseph Banks and Daniel Solander, presented to George III at Kew, and sent to Hertford to be inoculated against smallpox by Baron Thomas Dimsdale. For two years he was the most talked-about guest in fashionable London. This chapter has a hole at its centre. Mai left no writings of his own: no surviving firsthand account has been found, and none is known to have existed. Everything he is said to have said reaches the page through others, chiefly Fanny Burney, James Boswell (reporting Samuel Johnson), Captain Cook and the officers of the third voyage. His entries here are labelled as reported speech, and the reader should keep asking who is holding the pen. The return gaze survives only in fragments: Mai judging the Duchess of Devonshire's dress, Mai counting London's women on his fingers, Mai at Huahine asking for land to replace the estate his father lost to invaders from Bora Bora. The English record is mostly letters, a portrait, a biography and ships' journals, not diaries, and the form tags say so. Fanny Burney's letters to Samuel Crisp (first printed in 1889) are the liveliest: she admired his bows and table manners and used him to mock a lord's ill-bred son. Johnson's remark that there was little of the savage in him reaches us through Boswell's Life of 1791. Sandwich's letter about Mai's board and lodging, Solander's note that a ship was promised 'to carry Mr. Omai home', and Reynolds's great portrait complete the London side. The hosts' condescension is plain throughout: Mai is a curiosity, a ward, a test of whether manners are natural or taught; few of them asked what he wanted. What he wanted is reported consistently by those who sailed with him: firearms and help to drive the Bora Bora conquerors out of Raiatea and recover his family's land, and the standing that English goods might bring. Cook refused to join any such war and settled him instead on Huahine, in a house built by the ships' carpenters, with a horse and mare, muskets, pistols, a suit of armour given in England, and an inscription naming George III. The journals of Cook, James King, David Samwell, George Gilbert and James Burney record the settlement, the violence that surrounded it, and the farewell of 2 November 1777, when Mai broke down as he went ashore. The satirists had already moved in: 'An Historic Epistle from Omiah to the Queen of Otaheite' (1775) and 'Omiah's Farewell; inscribed to the Ladies of London' (1776) used his name to lampoon English society, and in December 1785 Covent Garden staged the pantomime 'Omai, or a Trip round the World'. places: Bengal, then London; claims to have sailed from Bengal in the same ship as Abu Taleb
Calcutta, the Cape, Cork and Dublin, London (lodgings in Gresse Street), Paris, Italy, Constantinople, Baghdad and the s
Cape Town, Cape of Good Hope

intro: In February 1799 Mirza Abu Taleb Khan, a Persian-writing administrator and poet from Lucknow, aged about forty-six and out of work in Calcutta, sailed for Europe on a Danish ship. His Scottish friend Captain David Richardson had promised to teach him English and pay his way. He went round the Cape, landed in Ireland in December, and reached London on 21 January 1800. For two and a half years he was a celebrity there, presented at court and asked to breakfasts, routs, masquerades and the Lord Mayor's feast. Crowds and newspapers called him 'the Persian Prince'. In June 1802, during the Peace of Amiens, he left for Paris and went home overland through Italy, Constantinople and Iraq. He reached Calcutta in August 1803. His own book, the Masir-i Talibi, is not a day-book. He wrote it up in India in 1804–05 from notes kept on the road, and it was printed in Persian at Calcutta only in 1812. Most readers met it in Charles Stewart's English translation of 1810. Stewart was a former Bengal officer who taught oriental languages at the East India Company's college near Hertford. The entries below are therefore dated passages from a travel account written up later and read in translation, and their form tags say so. Some passages carry exact dates, such as the mail coach out of Cork on 8 December 1799. Many fix only a season, and those are marked approximate. The hosts' side is thinner and mostly printed rather than private. The Morning Post reported the Duchess of Devonshire's gala breakfast in July 1800, and the Oracle reported the Lord Mayor's feast of November 1800, where by his own account he sat near Nelson. The Asiatic Annual Register printed his essay defending the liberties of Asian women. James Northcote painted him, and William Bond engraved the portrait for Stewart. Then came the reckoning of 1810–11. Stewart's preface presented him as an intelligent foreigner worth hearing, and the Quarterly and Eclectic Reviews weighed his book. Captain Thomas Williamson, a Bengal officer who said he had sailed in the same ship, used his East India Vade-Mecum to mock the Mirza's vanity, his title and his poetry. The gaze runs both ways and is often unkind. Abu Taleb found the Irish hospitable and quick but imprudent, and their villages like those of India. He listed twelve 'defects' of the English, beginning with want of religious faith and pride, and he thought Paris dirty and dark beside London. His hosts made him a prince he said he never claimed to be. They asked whether he had come to convert them, and in Williamson's case they accused him of ingratitude and of boasting about titled ladies. These judgements are given as each writer recorded them, without endorsing either side. Some records the reader might expect are missing here. No private diary of a London host describing him (Farington, Mrs Piozzi or others) could be confirmed for this chapter. title: The Imam and the Charter: Egyptian Students in Paris
eyes: Paris press (Moniteur universel, Revue encyclopédique, La Pandore, Gazette de France)
places: Alexandria, Marseilles, then Paris (rue de Clichy, later the mission house in rue du Regard and private lodgings)
Jardin du Roi (Jardin des Plantes), Paris

On foot from Marseilles via Lyon to Paris, May–June 1827
Paris embassy; in Dieppe during the July fighting
Paris: the mission house at 15 rue du Regard and the École des langues orientales

intro: On 13 April 1826 forty-four young men sailed from Alexandria on a French warship, sent by Muhammad Ali, the Ottoman governor of Egypt, to learn the sciences of the French. With them, as their imam, went a 25-year-old Azhar scholar, Rifa'a Rafi' al-Tahtawi. He was not meant to study. He did anyway, and his book about Paris, Takhlis al-ibriz fi talkhis Bariz ('The Extraction of Gold, or a Summary of Paris'), printed at Bulaq in 1834, became the founding Arabic text on modern Europe. The students reached Paris in the summer of 1826 and were placed under Edme-François Jomard, a veteran of Bonaparte's Egyptian expedition. They studied, sat public examinations, entered French schools and arsenals, and were written up in the official Moniteur, in liberal reviews and in satire. In the summer of 1827 the pasha's other envoy, a giraffe walked from Marseilles by Étienne Geoffroy Saint-Hilaire, outshone them all. Her keepers, Atir and Hassan, were drawn, stared at and paid, but left no account of their own. In July 1830 Tahtawi saw a French king overthrown in three days. He wrote a chapter on it and translated the Charter of 1814 whose breach had caused it, explaining French liberty through Islamic ideas of justice and equity, and reaching for an Upper Egyptian precedent to explain a republic. On the same days a young Berlioz was locked in the Institut writing a cantata, and an Austrian diplomat, Rodolphe Apponyi, was waiting in Dieppe for news. The record is uneven. Tahtawi's book is not a day-by-day diary but a topical account written up from notes and finished after his return, so most of its dates are those of the events it describes. The hosts' side is known through Jomard's printed reports, newspaper notices cited by historians, the letters of de Sacy and Caussin de Perceval printed in the Takhlis itself, and diaries and letters of Parisians who never mention the Egyptians at all. That silence is part of the picture: the students were news in 1826–28 and almost invisible by 1830. Read together, these sources show a two-way examination. Jomard and the orientalists judged the students' French and the accuracy of Tahtawi's account; Tahtawi judged French cleanliness, religion, women, newspapers and law, and his French readers in turn corrected some of his judgements before the book was printed.

title: Two-Sworded Princes on Broadway: The First Japanese Embassy to the United States

intro: In February 1860 the Tokugawa shogunate sent its first embassy to a Western country. Seventy-seven men under the envoy Shinmi Masaoki, the vice-envoy Muragaki Norimasa and the inspector (metsuke) Oguri Tadamasa sailed from Yokohama in the American steam frigate USS Powhatan, carrying the Japanese text of the 1858 Treaty of Amity and Commerce negotiated by Townsend Harris, to exchange ratifications in Washington. A Japanese-manned escort, the steam corvette Kanrin Maru under Kimura Yoshitake with Katsu Kaishū as captain, crossed separately to San Francisco with the castaway-turned-interpreter Nakahama Manjirō, a young retainer named Fukuzawa Yukichi, and an American naval officer, Lieutenant John Mercer Brooke, who had been shipwrecked in Japan and was going home. The embassy went by Honolulu, San Francisco and the Panama railway to Washington, landing at the Navy Yard on 14 May. President Buchanan received the envoys in the East Room on 17 May, ratifications were exchanged on 22 May, and the party then toured Baltimore, Philadelphia (where Oguri insisted on a whole-coin assay of Japanese and American gold at the Mint) and New York, where a procession up Broadway on 16 June drew enormous crowds and a poem from Walt Whitman. The envoys sailed home in USS Niagara on 30 June by the Cape Verde Islands, Luanda, Batavia and Hong Kong, reaching Edo in November: the first Japanese official party to go round the world. The gaze ran hard both ways. The Japanese diarists measured America against Confucian order and found it loud, egalitarian, oddly mixed in its sexes and careless of rank; Muragaki laughed at ballroom dancing, compared the Senate to a fish market, and privately thought samurai could beat these people, while also recording kindness, bouquets thrown from windows and a rooster in Honolulu that crowed just as cocks did at home. American newspapers read the visitors' faces, swords and manners with a physiognomist's eye, praised them as a 'wonderful people', worried that they might colonise, and turned a seventeen-year-old apprentice interpreter, Tateishi Onojirō, into 'Tommy', a celebrity of polkas and love letters. Lieutenant Brooke, aboard the Kanrin Maru, judged the Japanese crew harshly and Manjirō with near reverence. Most of the Japanese record is diaries kept on the voyage and copied out afterwards for circulation: Muragaki's (published in Japanese in 1918 and 1928; English translations 1920 and 1958), the Sendai retainer Tamamushi Sadayū's seven-volume 'Kōbei nichiroku' (unpublished until 1913), the navigational journal of the Kanrin Maru officer Akamatsu Noriyoshi, and the illustrated diary of Oguri's attendant Satō Tōshichi, a village headman, published only in 2001. Fukuzawa's vivid stories come from his autobiography dictated in 1897–99, nearly forty years on, and are marked as memoir. Brooke's journals stayed in his family until 1960. title: Half a Government Abroad: The Iwakura Embassy

intro: On 23 December 1871 a steamer left Yokohama carrying half the government of Japan. Iwakura Tomomi, the ambassador, took with him four vice-ambassadors: Kido Takayoshi, Ōkubo Toshimichi, Itō Hirobumi and Yamaguchi Masuka. With them went some fifty officials and secretaries and about sixty students. The students included five girls, the youngest of them Tsuda Ume, aged six, who would not see Japan again for eleven years. The embassy was meant to last ten months. It took twenty-one, and it went round the world. It had two purposes, and only one of them succeeded. The leaders hoped to begin revising the unequal treaties of 1858. In Washington, swayed by the warmth of their welcome, they tried to negotiate a new treaty at once, found they lacked full powers, and sent Ōkubo and Itō back across the Pacific to fetch them. When they returned, the moment had passed. The other purpose was to look: at mills, dockyards, schools, prisons, parliaments and slums. That one succeeded beyond anyone's plan. This chapter sets the travellers' records beside their hosts'. Kume Kunitake's five-volume official account (1878) is the spine. It is a worked-up record compiled after the return, not a day-book. Kido's private diary is the most candid Japanese voice; Ōkubo speaks only through his letters home; Itō's one great public speech was delivered in English. On the hosts' side are Hamilton Fish's diary of the failed talks, Grant's state papers, the welcomes of a Utah legislator and a Boston poet, the Queen's journal, and a string of British newspapers from London to Bradford. Most Japanese texts here survive only in Japanese or in modern translation, so they appear as digests. Quotations are limited to what was printed in English at the time: Itō's speech, Grant's message, Holmes's verse, the Spectator, the provincial press. Where a date or detail rests on a later study rather than on a fetched text, the entry says so. The best days are the ones when both sides wrote. On 4 March 1872 Grant welcomed a nation coming to learn, while Kume wondered at a head of state with no guards in ranks. On 25 October 1872 at Saltaire, a Bradford reporter counted the crowd while Kume counted the hours the mill children spent in school. And on 15 March 1873 Bismarck gave his guests a lesson in power, which Kume summarised and Ōkubo seems to have taken home.

title: The King of Kings Goes West: Naser al-Din Shah in Europe
places: Brussels, Dover, London, Windsor, Portsmouth, with the Shah
HMS Vigilant, Ostend to Dover; London
Tehran; then by Caspian, Volga and rail through Russia, Germany, Belgium, Britain, France, Switzerland, Italy, Austria,
With the Shah throughout the tour; dismissed on landing back in Gilan
intro: In the spring of 1873 Naser al-Din Shah Qajar, who had ruled Persia for a quarter of a century, left Tehran for a journey no Persian monarch had made: five months by steamer, rail and carriage through Russia, Germany, Belgium, Britain, France, Switzerland, Italy, Austria and the Ottoman Empire, and home through the Caucasus. The trip was the project of his grand vizier, Mirza Hosein Khan Moshir od-Dowleh, who hoped that seeing Europe would win the Shah to railways, ministries and law, and that foreign courts would back the vast concession he had just granted to Baron Julius de Reuter. The Shah kept a diary every day of the journey, and it was printed in Tehran on his return and translated into English by J. W. Redhouse in 1874. It is a plain, sometimes artless record of distances, meals, palaces, reviews, zoos and theatres, written by a king measuring other kings. It is also curious and frank: about Krupp's steam hammers and the soot of Manchester, the ruins of the Paris Commune, the poverty of southern Italy, and Russian improvements in a Tiflis that Persia had lost. His hosts wrote back. In London, Queen Victoria's journal, the India Office minder Owen Tudor Burne, the Spectator and Punch, a visiting Mark Twain and a member of the Commons all set down what they saw of him, often on the same days he was writing about them. In Berlin an American diplomat sent home a sharp report on his manners. The record on this side is mostly newspapers, comic weeklies, despatches, parliamentary debate and a later memoir rather than private diaries, and it is labelled that way here. Both sides' curiosity came mixed with condescension. London papers lectured each other on how to dazzle 'an Oriental', laughed at his table manners and later called his book schoolboyish; Punch made him a Persian cat. The Shah, for his part, read London crowds as personal devotion, judged peoples by their armies and their women, and wrote with the confidence of an absolute ruler. Behind the fireworks lay the Great Game: Britain courted Persia as a buffer against Russia, and Russia watched the courtship. At home the tour had a cost. Clergy led by Mulla Ali Kani and a court faction around the Shah's wife Anis od-Dowleh, sent home from Moscow, turned against the minister and his concession. When the royal party landed back in Gilan in September, Mirza Hosein Khan was dismissed, and the Reuter concession was cancelled before the year was out. By then a Petersburg columnist could call the whole journey old news.

title: The Envoy Who Wrote Too Much

A coastal fort (甲敦炮台) on an official visit
At sea Shanghai–Southampton (Dec 1876–Jan 1877), then the legation at 49 Portland Place, London; Paris in 1878
From Shanghai to Paris and London

intro: In February 1875 the British consular interpreter Augustus Margary was killed on the Yunnan–Burma border. The Chefoo Convention that Li Hongzhang signed with Sir Thomas Wade on 13 September 1876 settled the affair on British terms, and one term was a mission of apology to London. The man chosen was Guo Songtao, a 58-year-old Hunanese scholar who had long argued that China must understand the West. He was to deliver the apology and then stay: the first resident minister the Qing had ever posted to a Western capital. The court had ordered its envoys to keep diaries and send them home. Guo did so with unusual frankness. The voyage diary he posted from London in February 1877, Shi xi jicheng, praised the schools, prisons, ports and laws he had seen from Hong Kong to Southampton, and argued that the Western states had a civilisation of their own. The Zongli Yamen printed it; in June a court memorial called it disloyal, and the blocks were destroyed. For the next eighteen months Guo lived in Portland Place knowing that every line he wrote would be read in Beijing as evidence. This chapter sets the envoy's own diary beside those of his deputy Liu Xihong, who became his enemy, and his interpreter Zhang Deyi, who noticed bread, guest books and gadgets. Around them are the people who read and judged them: a patron in Tianjin, a memorialist and a diarist in Beijing, Punch, The Times, a Regent Street photographer, an Ipswich weekly, and the English papers of Hong Kong, Shanghai and Singapore. The record is mixed: diaries on the Chinese side, but also memorials, letters and newspapers, and on the British side mostly press and archive entries rather than private diaries. The clearest day is Sunday 25 March 1877, when all three Chinese diarists went to tea with the aged Earl Russell at Pembroke Lodge and each saw a different party; Guo talked with a four-year-old grandson who turned out to be Bertrand Russell. The longest thread runs from the ban of June 1877 to Liu's ten charges in 1878, as London newspapers explained to their readers why the envoy they found so reasonable was disgraced at home. Guo was recalled in August 1878. His successor Zeng Jize arrived in January 1879, and Guo went home to Hunan without reporting to the capital. His full diary waited a century to be published.

title: Sisters and Brothers: Asia Speaks in Chicago
eyes: American newspapers (Chicago Record, Inter Ocean, Dubuque Times, Critic, Midwest and Eastern papers)
places: Chicago (Art Institute, the Hale household on Dearborn Avenue); then lecture circuits in the Midwest, Detroit, New York,
Chicago, Hall of Columbus, Art Institute
Chicago, for The Critic, New York
Chicago; Madison; Des Moines; Detroit; Saginaw; Baltimore; New York
Colombo; London; Chicago; Honolulu on the way home
Hall of Columbus, Art Institute, Chicago
intro: In September 1893, beside the white plaster palaces of the World's Columbian Exposition, Chicago staged what its organisers called the first Parliament of the World's Religions. For seventeen days, in the new Art Institute on Michigan Avenue, clergy of every Christian denomination shared a platform with a Hindu monk, a Jain lawyer, Brahmo reformers, Buddhists from Ceylon and Japan, an envoy of the Chinese emperor and an American convert to Islam. Christians gave about 152 of the 194 papers; the handful of Asian speakers took most of the attention. The record is mostly speeches and letters rather than diaries. The speeches survive as printed by John Henry Barrows, the Presbyterian pastor who chaired the Parliament and edited its two-volume history, sometimes in condensed form; several of the visitors never spoke in English at all, and their words were read for them by Barrows or others. The fullest private voice is Vivekananda's, whose letters to his disciples in Madras and to his new American friends track his journey from penniless stranger to paid celebrity. Dharmapala kept diaries, published only in extracts; Pung Kwang Yu's paper went home as an official report to the throne. The hosts looked back through their own lenses. Barrows welcomed the 'wise men of the East' while holding that Christianity was the fulfilment of all faiths; the Archbishop of Canterbury refused to come at all. Newspapers in Chicago and in the small cities of the Midwest described the visitors' robes, turbans, voices and complexions before their arguments, swinging between admiration and racial condescension. Those descriptions are reported here as written. The visitors were not neutral either. Hirai Kinzō told the hall that Christian nations had imposed unequal treaties on Japan and barred Japanese children from American schools; Pung, Dharmapala and Vivekananda all charged missionaries with ignorance or arrogance. Vivekananda's letters praise American women and wealth and pour scorn on Indian caste, turning the comparison against his own country as much as his hosts'. A coda follows Vivekananda on the lecture circuit from Madison to Detroit to Baltimore, to a summer of teaching on the St Lawrence and to London and Oxford, where the gaze reverses again: the Indian monk calling on the European scholar who had interpreted India to the West.
